messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marco's Story

Marco Benedetti had been designing women's evening wear for twenty-three years when his daughter Elena died. She was twenty-six, a violinist, and she died in a car accident on a Tuesday evening in March—hit by a drunk driver while she was stopped at a red light on the way home from a rehearsal. The police told Marco that she would have died instantly. He had spent the first weeks after her funeral trying to decide whether to believe them.

What Marco remembers with absolute clarity is the moment he arrived at the hospital. The fluorescent hallway, the sound of his wife Lucia's voice breaking as she said Elena's name. The weight of her body when he held her in the morgue—already cold, already not his daughter. But the hours immediately before, the moment he received the call while standing in his studio surrounded by bolts of silk, those minutes are gone. He can see his assistant's face, pale and shocked, but cannot hear what words were used. He remembers driving to the hospital but not the route. These gaps terrify him, as if the missing pieces contain some crucial knowledge he should have had, some way he might have prevented what happened.

In the months that followed, whenever the memory surfaced—Elena's cold hand, the specific shade of the hospital's walls, his wife's raw voice—Marco felt consumed by guilt so intense it made his chest tight. If he had insisted she take a different route home. If he had driven her himself. If he had somehow known to keep her safe that evening. The guilt spiraled into a kind of panic, a certainty that he had failed her, that he was responsible, that he should have been able to protect her. These feelings were unbearable, and so he began to push them away. He would not allow himself to think about that Tuesday. Whenever the memory tried to surface, he would force his mind elsewhere—to a new design, to a client's demands, to anything that would keep the images and the crushing weight of guilt at bay.

But avoidance required constant vigilance. Marco threw himself into work with an intensity that alarmed his colleagues. He arrived at the studio before dawn and stayed until dark, sketching designs he never showed anyone, redesigning pieces that were already finished. He kept his mind occupied all the time, moving from task to task without pause, because the moment he stopped, the memory would creep in. He began to suppress any thought of the future—refused to discuss retirement with Lucia, wouldn't plan their anniversary trip, wouldn't even commit to next season's collection. Planning felt like a betrayal, as if imagining a future without Elena meant accepting that she was truly gone, that his failure was permanent. The thought of making any plans triggered a wave of dread and guilt that he couldn't tolerate.

What Marco hadn't anticipated was how the effort to avoid the memory would backfire. By refusing to think about Elena, by keeping his mind constantly occupied, he had inadvertently sensitized himself to her absence. Lucia would mention something—a piece of music on the radio, a young woman who looked like Elena passing on the street—and Marco's body would react before his mind could catch up. His heart would race, his hands would tremble, he would feel a sudden, overwhelming surge of panic and horror. These physical reactions were violent and involuntary, and they terrified him. His sleep had become impossible; he would lie awake beside Lucia, his body tense, his mind cycling through the same fragments of memory and guilt. When he did manage to sleep, he would wake gasping, drenched in sweat, the memory of that hospital hallway vivid and suffocating.

The physical reactions and the intrusive memories fed each other. A smell—perfume, gasoline, something indefinable—would trigger his racing heart, which would then pull the memory forward, which would then trigger the crushing guilt, which would then send him back to his avoidance strategies. He would work harder, distract himself more desperately, refuse to make any plans, anything to keep the guilt and the memories at bay. But the more he avoided, the more fragile his defenses became. After a year and a half of this, Lucia finally insisted he see someone. She said she was losing him, that she had already lost their daughter, and she couldn't lose him too. Marco knew she was right. He was exhausted, hollow, and terrified that if he stopped moving, if he stopped the constant distraction and suppression, the guilt and the memory would consume him entirely.
